note: Phases follow the published standards named in each discipline. Commands are the ones the tools in this catalogue actually produce; where a tool is not yet built, the command is still correct but has no page to link to.

frameworks.name: PTES
frameworks.summary: Seven phases covering a whole engagement, from the pre-engagement conversation to the report. The most widely used general structure, and the one most other methodologies slot into.

frameworks.name: OSSTMM 3
frameworks.full: Open Source Security Testing Methodology Manual
frameworks.summary: ISECOM's standard, and the only one here that is about measurement rather than findings. A RAV (Risk Assessment Value) scores attack surface against the controls protecting it, so two testers assessing the same target should land on comparable numbers. Reports go out in the STAR format. The four phases run over five channels, not just networks.

frameworks.name: OWASP WSTG
frameworks.summary: The reference for web testing. Every test has an identifier — WSTG-INFO-02, WSTG-ATHN-03 — which is what you cite in a report so a reader can look up exactly what you did.

frameworks.name: OWASP MASTG
frameworks.summary: The mobile counterpart, paired with MASVS which sets the requirement levels. Split by platform because the tooling barely overlaps.

frameworks.name: NIST SP 800-115
frameworks.full: Technical Guide to Information Security Testing
frameworks.summary: Technical Guide to Information Security Testing and Assessment. Broader than a pentest standard: a pentest is one technique among several. Execution runs four technique categories in order of impact, passive to active, and not every engagement needs to reach the last one. Guidance, not regulation — it mandates no testing frequency, unlike PCI DSS.

frameworks.name: CREST
frameworks.summary: Less a test methodology than a standard for how the engagement is run: scoping, consent, tester competence, evidence handling, reporting quality. What a client buys when they buy a CREST-accredited test.

frameworks.name: PCI DSS 4.0
frameworks.summary: Compliance-driven, so the rules are specific: at least annually and after any significant change, internal and external, network and application layer, plus explicit segmentation testing at least every six months.

frameworks.name: ISSAF
frameworks.summary: OISSG, v0.2.1, last published around 2006 and no longer maintained — there is no official download left. Worth knowing for the nine-step assessment model inside its middle phase, which is still the clearest map of how an attacker actually progresses: steps 1-3 recon, 4-7 active compromise, 8-9 persistence and stealth. Study the logic, not its tool advice.

frameworks.name: MITRE ATT&CK
frameworks.full: Adversarial Tactics, Techniques and Common Knowledge
frameworks.summary: Not a test methodology — a shared vocabulary for what attackers do. You map findings to it so a blue team can say which techniques they would have caught.

frameworks.name: CSA CCM
frameworks.summary: Cloud Security Alliance. A governance and compliance control set, not a testing methodology: 17 domains mapped across ISO 27001, NIST and PCI DSS. Reach for it when a client wants to know whether their cloud configuration meets a standard, rather than whether you can break into it.

frameworks.name: CBEST
frameworks.summary: Bank of England, with the UK financial sector. Starts with a bespoke threat intelligence phase that names the threat actors relevant to that specific institution, and the test then simulates those scenarios. Regulator-backed, and nothing general-purpose substitutes for it when a UK bank is in scope.

frameworks.name: WASC TC
frameworks.summary: Web Application Security Consortium. A taxonomy for naming web attack classes that mattered in the mid-2000s and has since been superseded by the OWASP Top Ten and WSTG. You will meet it in old reports and in compliance documents that were never rewritten.

disciplines.name: Web application
disciplines.summary: Follows the OWASP Web Security Testing Guide. Each phase cites its WSTG identifier so a finding can be traced back to a published test.

phases.name: Map the application
phases.goal: Know what exists before testing any of it. Most missed findings are on pages nobody knew were there.

steps.what: Fingerprint the server, framework and technologies
steps.why: Version information narrows everything that follows, and sometimes is the finding.

steps.what: Find content that is not linked
steps.why: Admin panels, backups, old versions and .git directories are found here or not at all.

steps.what: Enumerate virtual hosts and subdomains
steps.why: One address often serves several sites, and the forgotten one is usually the weak one.

phases.name: Configuration and deployment
phases.goal: The platform underneath the application, which is frequently where the real issue is.

steps.what: Check TLS and certificates
steps.why: Expired, self-signed and weak-cipher findings are easy to prove and easy to fix.

steps.what: Look for exposed files and methods
steps.why: Backup files, version control and dangerous HTTP methods are configuration mistakes, not code bugs.

phases.name: Authentication and session
phases.goal: How the application decides who you are, and whether it keeps deciding correctly.

steps.what: Examine the login and session cookies
steps.why: Missing Secure, HttpOnly or SameSite flags are findings on their own.

steps.what: Test credential handling, with permission
steps.why: Rate limiting and lockout behaviour is part of the control, not an obstacle to testing it.
steps.warn: Will lock accounts. Agree this in scope first, in writing.

phases.name: Input validation
phases.goal: Everything the application accepts from outside, which is where injection lives.

steps.what: Find parameters that are not advertised
steps.why: Debug and legacy parameters survive long after the UI that used them.

steps.what: Test for SQL injection
steps.why: Still among the highest-impact findings when it is there.
steps.warn: Intrusive. --risk 3 can modify data. Only in scope, only with written permission.

phases.name: Report
phases.goal: A finding nobody can reproduce is not a finding.

steps.what: Record the exact command, output and timestamp for every finding
steps.why: Reproducibility is what separates a report from an assertion, and CREST assesses you on it.

disciplines.name: Network and infrastructure
disciplines.summary: PTES for the shape of the engagement, NIST SP 800-115 for the four-phase structure clients recognise, OSSTMM where measurement matters.

phases.name: Discovery
phases.goal: What is alive, and what is listening on it.

steps.what: Find live hosts without scanning everything
steps.why: Scanning a /16 port by port wastes hours. Sweep first, then scan what answered.

steps.what: Enumerate ports and services
steps.why: The service and its version drive everything after this.

phases.name: Vulnerability analysis
phases.goal: Turn a service list into a list of things worth trying.

steps.what: Run the script checks against what you found
steps.why: NSE covers a large amount of known ground cheaply.

steps.what: Inspect traffic where the protocol matters
steps.why: Plaintext protocols are proved by capture, not by assertion.

phases.name: Attack
phases.goal: Prove the finding, take only what the scope allows.
phases.warn: Everything in this phase needs written authorisation naming the systems in scope.

steps.what: Validate credentials and access
steps.why: A theoretical finding and a demonstrated one land very differently in a report.

phases.name: Report
phases.goal: Evidence a third party can re-run.

steps.what: Save machine-readable output alongside the narrative
steps.why: XML and JSON feed the report; the normal output is what a reader checks.

disciplines.name: Mobile
disciplines.summary: OWASP MASTG, with MASVS setting the level you are testing against. Android and iOS share a structure and almost no tooling.

phases.name: Gather the artefacts
phases.goal: Get the package and know what is inside it before testing anything.

steps.what: Pull the application package from a device
steps.why: You test the build that ships, not the one in the repository.

cmds.text: adb shell pm list packages | grep target

steps.what: Unpack and read the manifest
steps.why: Exported components, permissions, backup and cleartext settings are all declared here.

phases.name: Storage and cryptography
phases.goal: What the application keeps, and how badly it keeps it.

steps.what: Look for secrets in the package and on disk
steps.why: Hard-coded keys and tokens are still among the most common mobile findings.

phases.name: Network
phases.goal: What it sends, to whom, and whether anyone can read it.

steps.what: Intercept and inspect the traffic
steps.why: Certificate pinning, cleartext endpoints and over-collection all show up here.

disciplines.name: Cloud and containers
disciplines.summary: No single standard owns this yet. PTES gives the shape; the provider's own benchmark gives the checks; ATT&CK gives the vocabulary for what you demonstrate.

phases.name: Enumerate what is exposed
phases.goal: Public storage and forgotten endpoints, found from outside.

steps.what: Look for readable buckets
steps.why: Open object storage remains one of the most common and most serious cloud findings.

phases.name: Container and image review
phases.goal: What a container can reach, and what it was built from.

steps.what: Inspect how containers are run
steps.why: Privileged containers, mounted sockets and host networking are the usual escapes.

steps.what: Show what hardening looks like
steps.why: A finding is more useful next to the configuration that fixes it.

disciplines.name: Wireless
disciplines.summary: OSSTMM treats wireless as its own channel, which is the right model — the medium is shared, so scope and legality are tighter than anywhere else.

phases.name: Survey
phases.goal: What is broadcasting, and which of it is yours to test.
phases.warn: Capturing traffic you are not authorised to capture is an offence in most jurisdictions. Scope wireless in writing, with SSIDs and physical boundaries named.

steps.what: Enumerate networks and clients
steps.why: You cannot scope what you have not surveyed.

steps.what: Analyse a capture you are entitled to
steps.why: Reading a capture is where the finding is proved.

disciplines.name: PCI DSS
disciplines.summary: Requirement 11.4. The structure is set by the standard rather than by you, and the segmentation test is the part people forget.

phases.name: Define the cardholder data environment
phases.goal: Everything that stores, processes or transmits card data, plus everything connected to it.

steps.what: Inventory the in-scope hosts and their services
steps.why: The scope boundary is the finding if it is wrong.

phases.name: Segmentation testing
phases.goal: Prove the CDE is isolated from everything out of scope. Required at least every six months.

steps.what: Attempt to reach the CDE from an out-of-scope segment
steps.why: The requirement is to demonstrate isolation, which means showing the attempt and the failure.

phases.name: External and internal testing
phases.goal: Both perspectives, at network and application layer, annually and after significant change.

steps.what: Test the external perimeter
steps.why: Required separately from the internal test; findings differ.

steps.what: Test the application layer
steps.why: 11.4.3 and 11.4.4 both require application-layer testing, not just a port scan.

choosing.intro: Nobody picks one framework and uses it for everything. A real engagement has a primary methodology that structures the work, plus whatever the client's industry, platform or regulator forces on top. Four things decide it.

criteria.name: What you are testing
criteria.detail: The first and bluntest filter. A web app points at OWASP WSTG. A mobile app points at MASTG. A whole corporate network points at PTES or OSSTMM. A scope that includes people and buildings, not just hosts, points at OSSTMM and its five channels.

criteria.name: What the regulator says
criteria.detail: This overrides what you would have preferred. Cardholder data means PCI DSS Requirement 11.4, whatever else you run. A UK bank under Bank of England oversight means CBEST. A US federal system means NIST SP 800-115 carries the weight.

criteria.name: Whether the numbers have to be comparable
criteria.detail: If the client wants to compare this year to last year, or compare two different firms, you need a measurement layer. That is what OSSTMM's RAVs are for, and no other framework here gives you it.

criteria.name: What your team can actually run
criteria.detail: The constraint people skip. A full OSSTMM needs real fluency in its metrics. CBEST needs a threat intelligence capability. For a small team on a standard network job, PTES gives the structure without the overhead.

scenarios.q: A regional hospital wants its patient portal and the internal network behind it tested. HIPAA applies. Payments are outsourced. The board wants a summary it can read.
scenarios.why: It covers the whole engagement end to end, and its reporting phase explicitly produces both an executive summary and a technical report, which is exactly what a board plus an IT team needs. Use OWASP WSTG for the portal test cases, and tag the findings with MITRE ATT&CK technique IDs so the security team can go and build detections.

scenarios.q: A multinational bank headquartered in London needs a test that satisfies its UK regulator, starting from a threat intelligence assessment of that institution.
scenarios.why: It is built for UK financial institutions, it mandates the bespoke threat intelligence phase they are describing, and it is the one the Bank of England recognises. No general-purpose framework satisfies that on its own.

scenarios.q: A SaaS startup wants two different security firms to test its web platform over two years and compare the results directly to see whether it improved.
scenarios.a: OSSTMM for the measurement, WSTG for the tests.
scenarios.why: 'Did we improve?' is a measurement question, and RAVs are the only thing here that makes two separate firms' results comparable. WSTG supplies the web test cases underneath that measurement layer.

scenarios.q: A fintech wants its Android and iOS banking apps tested. Both handle card transactions.
scenarios.why: MASTG gives you the mobile test cases for both platforms. PCI DSS applies the moment cardholder data is in play, and it is not optional. You satisfy the testing methodology and the regulatory mandate at the same time.

scenarios.q: A US federal agency wants its internal network assessed, aligned to federal guidance, covering document review as well as active testing.
scenarios.why: It is the federally recognised one, and it is deliberately broader than a pentest standard: its execution phase runs from reviewing policies and firewall rules through to exploitation, so document review and active testing live in the same methodology.

scenarios.q: An e-commerce company has a web storefront, a mobile shopping app, and a payment system.
scenarios.why: Three components, three references. WSTG for the storefront, MASTG for the app, and PCI DSS over the top because the payment system puts cardholder data in scope. PTES underneath keeps the engagement itself structured.
